Newborn Care

Lumbar puncture in a newborn: tests, comfort and aftercare

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Hearing that your baby needs a lumbar puncture can be frightening. The test takes a small sample of the fluid around the brain and spinal cord. The neonatal team should explain why it is needed, how they will keep your baby comfortable and safe, and how the result may change treatment.

What fluid is being sampled?

Cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, surrounds the brain and spinal cord. A lumbar puncture, also called an LP or spinal tap, collects some of this fluid through a needle between the bones of the lower back. The team chooses a level below the end of the spinal cord. It is not a bone-marrow sample and is not intended to put a needle into the spinal cord itself.

A common reason in newborn care is concern about meningitis, an infection or inflammation affecting the coverings of the brain and spinal cord. Blood tests alone cannot always establish whether these tissues are involved. In selected cases, CSF is examined for other neurological or metabolic problems; the team should explain the particular question for your baby.

When is the test appropriate?

Not every baby with a possible infection needs exactly the same investigations. NICE recommends lumbar puncture when there is strong suspicion of neonatal infection or signs suggesting meningitis, provided it is safe. Before proceeding, clinicians assess breathing, circulation, neurological signs and bleeding risk, and consider infection at the needle site or signs of dangerously raised pressure. A scan is not automatically required for every baby.

A baby with an unsafe airway, breathing problems, shock or uncontrolled seizures needs treatment and stabilization first. Ideally, samples are taken before antibiotics because treatment can affect results, but an LP must not delay urgently needed antibiotics in a seriously unwell baby. If antibiotics have already started, the team may still obtain a useful sample when it becomes safe.

What do the laboratory tests show?

Tests can include red and white cell counts, protein and glucose, with a blood glucose sample taken at about the same time for comparison. Microscopy, bacterial culture and antibiotic-sensitivity testing, and PCR for relevant germs answer different questions. Some viruses, fungi or metabolic conditions need selected additional tests; routine culture does not detect every possible cause. Results depend on the baby’s gestational and postnatal age, other findings and any antibiotics already given.

Some initial results may be available within hours; cultures and other tests take longer, with local laboratory times varying. A normal-looking or clear sample, a single normal cell count or a negative culture after antibiotics does not by itself exclude meningitis. Ask which results are available, what remains uncertain and how long treatment or hospital observation is expected to continue. Do not stop antibiotics while waiting for a result unless the treating team changes the plan.

Preparing together with the neonatal team

The team should discuss the reason for the LP, likely benefits, possible difficulties or complications and the options if a sample cannot be obtained. Tell them about relevant medicines, allergies or previous reactions. They prepare a warm clinical area, appropriate monitoring, sterile equipment and a skin-cleaning solution suitable for the baby’s age and skin. Equipment choice and specimen requirements are professional decisions.

Ask whether you can stay, speak softly or help comfort your baby in a way staff consider safe. You do not have to watch if you find it upsetting. Ask specifically about feeding before and after the test, particularly if sedation or significant illness is involved. Do not impose a fast, try to empty the stomach or change feeding yourself based on a general procedure checklist. If you are unsure about consent, ask a senior clinician to explain the risks of testing and of proceeding without a diagnostic sample.

Pain relief and comfort matter

Newborns feel pain, and being held still can also cause distress. The team may use supportive holding, a familiar pacifier, appropriately supervised breast milk or a small prescribed sucrose preparation, and local anaesthetic when suitable. These measures may be combined; the choice depends on the baby’s condition and how urgent the sample is. Crying does not mean that nothing has been done for pain, but staff should keep assessing comfort.

Some babies need additional medicines under specialist supervision; sedation is not an automatic part of every newborn LP. It can affect breathing and feeding readiness, so monitoring must fit the medicines and the baby’s health. Do not apply numbing cream, give pain medicine, sedatives or homemade sugar water unless the neonatal team specifically directs it. Ask how they will recognize pain and what they will do if your baby is not tolerating the procedure.

What happens during the procedure?

A trained assistant supports the baby, either on the side or in a supported sitting position, while protecting the airway and keeping the baby warm. A large neonatal trial found better sampling success with sitting than lying, mainly in term babies under three days old; it did not guarantee success in every baby. The clinician chooses a safe position for the individual baby. Parents should not try to reproduce procedural holding or bend the neck forward themselves.

After sterile skin preparation, the clinician uses a specially designed needle to collect drops of fluid into sterile tubes, then removes the needle and applies a small dressing. The amount and tests are selected by the team. Breathing, heart rate and oxygen levels may be monitored, with pauses or a change of plan if needed. This is a professional procedure; needle size, direction and depth are not steps for a parent to carry out.

If the sample is bloody or cannot be obtained

Sometimes no fluid is obtained, there is too little for all tests, or blood mixes with the sample. This does not automatically mean the baby has a new disease or a spinal injury. Blood can make interpretation difficult; some tests may still be useful. The team reviews the result and may seek a more experienced clinician, consider another attempt or use imaging assistance in selected circumstances.

Discuss what another attempt would change and how comfort will be managed. If no reliable sample is available, treatment for presumed meningitis may need to continue rather than assuming infection has been excluded. Small bleeding or bruising and temporary soreness can occur; serious infection, bleeding around the spine or nerve injury are rare. The team assesses individual risks and uses precautions, but no procedure has a guaranteed zero risk.

When fluid is removed for another purpose

Some premature babies develop enlarged fluid spaces after bleeding in the brain. Specialists may occasionally use lumbar puncture as one temporary way to remove fluid or obtain a sample. That is a different decision from a diagnostic infection test and depends on the anatomy, pressure, scans and wider treatment plan.

Routine repeated LPs are not recommended simply to prevent progression of posthaemorrhagic hydrocephalus or avoid a shunt. Other temporary drainage procedures or later surgery may be needed. Ask which problem is being treated, the goal and how progress will be checked; there is no universal drainage volume or schedule for parents to apply.

Aftercare, feeding and observation

The team checks recovery, comfort and the puncture site, and explains feeding, bathing and dressing care. Monitoring depends on illness, prematurity, breathing and any sedating medicines, rather than a universal one- or four-hour limit. If sedation was used, the team decides when the baby is alert and safe enough to feed. Do not assume that every baby must avoid milk for two hours or can feed immediately regardless of their clinical plan.

Routine flat bed rest has not been shown to prevent post-LP headache in children, so a mandatory hour lying flat is not a proven rule for that purpose. Follow the neonatal unit’s recovery instructions. Older children may report headache or back soreness; a newborn’s persistent distress or behaviour change needs assessment, not an assumption that it is merely a headache. Give only pain medicine specifically prescribed or advised for this baby, and ask when the dressing may be removed or the baby bathed.

Know the results and warning-sign plan

Before discharge, ask who will explain pending results, whether medicines continue, the follow-up date and which service to call at any hour. Contact the neonatal team promptly for feeding changes, repeated vomiting, persistent distress or a puncture site that becomes red, swollen, bleeds or leaks fluid. Report ongoing leakage promptly, and do not assume new illness is a normal result of the LP.

Get immediate emergency help for breathing difficulty or pauses, blue/grey or unusually pale or mottled colour, a seizure, difficulty waking or unresponsiveness, or a rash that does not fade under pressure. A newborn with a temperature of 38°C or higher or below 36°C needs immediate hospital assessment, even after a reassuring test. A weak, unusually high-pitched or continuous cry or a baby who seems seriously unwell also needs immediate help. In hospital, alert staff at once; at home, use local emergency services when needed rather than waiting for results or the next appointment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask why the sample is needed, what the result may change, and how safety and pain relief will be managed.

Get the feeding and aftercare plan from the neonatal team rather than applying fixed times or medicines from a general checklist.

Keep the pending-result contact, medicine plan and urgent warning signs in writing; new illness must not wait for the next appointment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help keep procedure dates, feeding observations, prescribed medicines, pending results and appointment questions together. It cannot decide whether an LP is safe, interpret a newborn’s CSF, prescribe pain relief or replace immediate clinical care.

When to seek help

Alert staff immediately or seek emergency care for breathing problems, blue/grey or unusually pale or mottled colour, a seizure, reduced responsiveness or a non-fading rash. A newborn temperature of 38°C or higher or below 36°C needs immediate hospital assessment. Weak, unusually high-pitched or continuous crying or a seriously unwell appearance also needs immediate help. Contact the treating team promptly for feeding problems, persistent distress or a bleeding, leaking, red or swollen puncture site. Do not perform procedural holding, change medicines or impose fasting yourself.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • An LP samples fluid around the nervous system; it is not a bone-marrow test or an injection into the spinal cord.
  • The reason, timing and safety depend on the baby’s condition; urgent treatment must not wait for the procedure.
  • Comfort, professional positioning and monitoring are planned for the individual newborn.
  • A bloody or unsuccessful sample may need reassessment; one result alone cannot always exclude infection.
  • Ask for feeding, aftercare, pending-result and emergency instructions before leaving the neonatal service.

Frequently asked questions

Why might my baby need a lumbar puncture?

A common reason is concern about meningitis. CSF can add information that blood tests alone cannot provide. Not every baby needs the same tests; the team should explain the specific reason and whether it is safe now.

What tests are done on the fluid?

They may include cell counts, protein, glucose compared with blood glucose, microscopy, culture and PCR for selected germs. Other tests depend on the question. Age, blood contamination and prior antibiotics affect interpretation.

Must a newborn always lie on their side?

No. Clinicians may use supported sitting or side-lying. A large trial mainly involving term babies under three days found better success with sitting, but positioning must still protect each baby’s airway and stability. Staff perform the holding.

Does a failed attempt mean something is wrong with the spine?

Not necessarily. Obtaining enough usable fluid can be difficult. The team reassesses, may ask a more experienced colleague or consider another approach, and explains how treatment continues if meningitis cannot be confidently excluded.

Can my baby be fed after the test?

Ask the neonatal team for the individual plan. Feeding readiness depends on the baby’s illness, breathing and any sedation; neither a blanket two-hour fast nor automatic immediate feeding suits every baby.

Does lying flat for an hour prevent headache?

Routine bed rest has not shown preventive benefit in children. Follow the unit’s recovery and monitoring plan; persistent newborn distress, poor feeding or behaviour change needs assessment rather than being dismissed as a headache.

When will the result be ready?

Some initial findings can return within hours, while cultures and other tests take longer. Ask what is pending and who will contact you. Antibiotics may reduce culture yield, and a single normal result does not always exclude infection.

What changes need emergency help?

Breathing difficulty or pauses, blue/grey or unusually pale or mottled colour, seizures, difficulty waking, unresponsiveness or a non-fading rash need immediate emergency care. A newborn temperature of at least 38°C or below 36°C needs immediate hospital assessment. A weak, unusually high-pitched or continuous cry or a seriously unwell appearance also needs immediate help. Alert hospital staff at once or seek emergency help from home.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
